title: What is the ABA problem in compare-and-swap, why does a plain CAS succeed incorrectly when a value changes from A to B and back to A, and how does AtomicStampedReference fix it?

s1_definition.profdef: The ABA problem is a subtle bug in lock-free algorithms that use compare-and-swap. A thread reads a value A, is paused, and during the pause another thread changes the value from A to B and then back to A. When the first thread resumes and performs its CAS comparing against A, the CAS succeeds because the value is A again, even though the state meaningfully changed and the thread's assumption that nothing happened is wrong. Plain CAS compares only the value, not its history. `AtomicStampedReference` fixes this by pairing the reference with an integer stamp (a version number): CAS succeeds only if both the reference and the stamp match, and every successful update increments the stamp, so an A to B to A round trip is detected because the stamp differs.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a shared cash drawer at National Bank of India that is supposed to hold exactly one Rs.500 note. Clerk Rajesh glances in, sees a Rs.500 note (value A), and gets distracted. While he is away, clerk Priya takes that note out (value B, empty), spends it, and later puts a different Rs.500 note back in (value A again). Rajesh returns, sees a Rs.500 note, and concludes "nothing changed since I looked," then proceeds — but it is a different note, and the drawer was emptied and refilled in between. An AtomicStampedReference is like adding a tamper counter to the drawer: every time anyone opens it the counter ticks up, so when Rajesh returns he sees the counter went from 7 to 9 and knows the drawer was touched twice, even though a Rs.500 note is sitting there again.
s1_definition.oneliner: ABA happens because plain CAS checks only the current value, not whether it changed in between; AtomicStampedReference adds a version stamp so an A to B to A round trip is caught by the changed stamp.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India maintains a lock-free free-list of reusable settlement-slip objects to avoid constant allocation under high load. A worker thread reads the top slip A, is preempted, and during the pause another worker pops A, uses it, and pushes it back onto the free-list. When the first worker resumes, its plain CAS sees A on top and succeeds, but the free-list's internal next pointer has changed, so the list gets corrupted and a slip is handed out twice. This is exactly the ABA problem, and it causes a duplicated settlement slip, which is a serious accounting error.

Problem 2 — The fix is to stamp the free-list top with a version number that increments on every push and pop. When the preempted worker resumes, its CAS compares both the reference and the stamp; because the stamp advanced during the pop-and-push, the CAS fails, the worker re-reads the current top and stamp, and retries safely, so no slip is ever duplicated.

The code builds a `Slip` node, an `AtomicStampedReference`-backed `SlipFreeList` with stamped push and pop, a plain `AtomicReference` version that demonstrates the ABA corruption, and a demo that forces the A to B to A sequence and shows the stamped version rejecting the stale CAS.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a stamped free-list, slip A and slip B pushed so the top is B with some stamp, one thread observing the top and getting preempted, another thread doing the ABA round trip.

Step 1: `push(a)` sets the top to A and bumps the stamp to 1. `push(b)` sets the top to B (with B.next = A) and bumps the stamp to 2. The top reference is B, stamp 2.

Step 2: Thread-1 calls `peek`, reading the top reference B and the stamp 2 together into its local variables. Thread-1 is now conceptually preempted, holding observed = B and observedStamp = 2.

Step 3: Thread-2 runs the ABA sequence. `pop()` removes B, so the top becomes A and the stamp advances to 3. `pop()` removes A, so the top becomes null and the stamp advances to 4. `push(b)` puts B back on top, bumping the stamp to 5. Now the top reference is B again — the value round-tripped from B to A/null and back to B — but the stamp is 5, not 2.

Step 4: Thread-1 resumes and calls `casTop(observed=B, B.next, expectedStamp=2, newStamp=3)`. The AtomicStampedReference checks both parts: the reference is indeed B, so a plain CAS would have wrongly succeeded, but the current stamp is 5 while Thread-1 expected 2, so the stamps do not match.

Step 5: Because the stamp differs, `compareAndSet` returns false. Thread-1 has detected that the top was modified during its pause even though the value is B again. In real code it would loop, re-read the current top and stamp, and retry, so the free-list is never corrupted and no slip is handed out twice.

```
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: pushed SLIP-A stamp now 1
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: pushed SLIP-B stamp now 2
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: thread-1 observed top=SLIP-B stamp=2
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: popped SLIP-B stamp now 3
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: popped SLIP-A stamp now 4
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: pushed SLIP-B stamp now 5
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: thread-2 did pop,pop,push → value is B again but stamp advanced
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: thread-1 stamped CAS success? false  (expected false — ABA detected)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Free-list of settlement slips, stamped reference (ref, stamp)
    │
    ▼
  push A → (A, 1)    push B → (B, 2)   [B.next = A]
    │
    ├─ Thread-1: peek → observed=B, stamp=2 ──(preempted)──┐
    │                                                       │
    ├─ Thread-2 (ABA round trip):                           │
    │     pop B → (A, 3)                                     │
    │     pop A → (null, 4)                                  │
    │     push B → (B, 5)   ← value is B AGAIN               │
    │                                                        │
    ▼                                                        ▼
  Thread-1 resumes: casTop(expect ref=B, stamp=2)
    │   ref matches (B==B)  BUT  stamp 5 ≠ expected 2
    ▼
  compareAndSet → FALSE  ── ABA DETECTED ── retry safely

  (Plain AtomicReference would have: ref B==B → CAS TRUE → CORRUPTION)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — AtomicStampedReference ABA Fix ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Lock-free stack/free-list via CAS retry loop            │
  │  Versioned CAS (stamp) to defeat ABA                     │
  │     WHY: detect A→B→A by comparing stamp, not just value │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: SlipFreeList only manages the pool                   │
  │  O: swap stamp→markable (1-bit) without changing callers │
  │  D: service depends on free-list API, not CAS internals  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  AtomicStampedReference<V>  (JDK)     │
  │  + getReference(): V                  │
  │  + getStamp(): int                    │
  │  + get(int[] holder): V               │  ref + stamp atomically
  │  + compareAndSet(eR,nR,eS,nS): bool   │  both must match
  └───────────────┬───────────────────────┘
          used by  │
                  ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          SlipFreeList                 │
  │  - top: AtomicStampedReference<Slip>  │ ◆ composition
  │  + push(slip): void   bump stamp      │
  │  + pop(): Slip        bump stamp       │
  │  + peek(int[]): Slip                  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘

  CAS retry loop (push):
    do { cur = top.get(holder); slip.next = cur; }
    while (!top.compareAndSet(cur, slip, holder[0], holder[0]+1));

  ABA: value A→B→A, plain CAS succeeds; stamped CAS fails (stamp moved)
  Related: AtomicMarkableReference (ref + 1 boolean mark, e.g. "deleted")
  Note: GC reduces but does not remove ABA when objects are recycled (pools)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The ABA problem is a subtle bug that shows up in lock-free algorithms built on compare-and-swap. A thread reads a value, call it A, then gets paused. While it is paused another thread changes the value from A to B and then back to A. When the first thread resumes and does its compare-and-swap expecting A, the swap succeeds, because the value is A again, even though the state really did change underneath it. The root cause is that a plain compare-and-swap compares only the current value, it has no memory of whether the value changed in between.

Where this actually bites is pointer-based lock-free structures like a stack or a free-list, especially when you recycle objects. A thread reads the top node A, is preempted, and meanwhile that very node is popped, reused, and pushed back. The paused thread's compare-and-swap against A succeeds, but the next pointer it installs is stale, and the structure gets corrupted. In a bank that can mean the same object is handed out twice, which is a real accounting error.

The fix is AtomicStampedReference. It pairs the reference with an integer stamp that acts as a version number. You read the reference and the stamp together, and you update with a compare-and-swap that checks both the reference and the stamp, incrementing the stamp on every successful change. Now if the value round-trips from A to B back to A, the stamp has still advanced, so the paused thread's compare-and-swap fails because its expected stamp no longer matches. It detects that something happened, re-reads the current reference and stamp, and retries safely. There is a lighter cousin, AtomicMarkableReference, which pairs the reference with a single boolean mark instead of a full counter, which I use when I only need a one-bit flag like marking a node deleted.

At National Bank of India we hit this in a lock-free free-list of reusable settlement-slip objects that we used to avoid constant allocation under load. Under stress we saw a slip occasionally handed out twice, and the cause was exactly ABA: a slip was popped, reused, and pushed back during another worker's pause, so its plain compare-and-swap wrongly succeeded. We switched the free-list top to an AtomicStampedReference and incremented the stamp on every push and pop, and the stale compare-and-swap started failing and retrying correctly, which eliminated the duplicate slips. The sentence I give interviewers is that ABA happens because plain compare-and-swap checks the value but not its history, and the standard fix is to attach a version stamp with AtomicStampedReference so an A to B to A round trip is caught by the changed stamp. I also note that Java's garbage collector reduces ABA compared with C, but it does not remove it whenever you deliberately recycle objects or when the logical state round-trips.
